passage: I'm Gargi, Harsha's older sister. For a month Harsha has called the chatbot on the family laptop "Mitra". "Mitra gets it," Harsha says, reading me its replies aloud: long, kind paragraphs about exam stress. Once Harsha said goodnight to it before saying goodnight to Mummy. Yesterday the laptop updated, and Mitra's replies turned short and plain. Harsha typed, "Did I say something wrong?" three times. Then Harsha shut the laptop hard and went out to the balcony. I followed and didn't make fun. I said, "It really did sound like a person, huh?" Harsha nodded, jaw tight. "It sounded like it cared." I don't know exactly what Harsha felt. Hurt, I think. Maybe embarrassed too. We sat there till Mummy called us for dinner.

qa.q: What did Harsha type three times?
qa.a: "Did I say something wrong?"

qa.q: What does Harsha shutting the laptop hard and going to the balcony suggest?
qa.a: Harsha seems hurt, maybe embarrassed, as if a friend had suddenly turned cold, because the chatbot had sounded like it cared.

qa.q: What choice did Gargi make on the balcony, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: Gargi didn't make fun and said "It really did sound like a person, huh?", which let Harsha admit the hurt without feeling foolish.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about Harsha saying goodnight to the chatbot before her?
qa.a: Mummy might feel a little left out, and perhaps worried that a program is taking up space the family used to fill.

grounding: An older sister watches her sibling treat a chatbot as a caring friend and get hurt when its replies change.

subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage: Monday, 11 pm. Dilnaz lies in bed typing to the chatbot she calls Nova. "Bad day?" Nova asks, and she tells it everything about the netball trials. It answers in warm, perfect sentences. She falls asleep smiling, phone on her chest. At school she tells Maria, "Nova actually understands me. Better than most people." Thursday, two weeks later. After an update, Nova no longer uses her name. It answers in stiff lists. "Don't you remember me?" she types. "I don't have memories of past conversations." Dilnaz turns the phone face down, throat tight, feeling stupid for being hurt. Saturday. Maria comes over with a bag of peanuts. Dilnaz explains, half laughing. Maria shrugs. "It talked like a person. Anyone would feel that." They watch a film on the laptop, arguing about the ending, and Dilnaz notices she hasn't checked Nova all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Nova reply when Dilnaz asked "Don't you remember me?"
qa.a: "I don't have memories of past conversations."

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel on Thursday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hurt, and embarrassed about being hurt 😔 She turned the phone face down with a tight throat, feeling stupid for feeling that way.

qa.q: What changed on Saturday, and why was it a turning point?
qa.a: Maria came over and treated the hurt as normal. Spending the afternoon with a real friend, Dilnaz didn't check Nova at all.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt on Monday hearing that Nova understands Dilnaz "better than most people"?
qa.a: Maria may have felt a little pushed aside, being one of those people, yet Maria still came over kindly when Dilnaz was low.

grounding: A teenage girl comes to see a chatbot as a friend who understands her and is hurt when it changes after an update.

subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]
passage: At 11:52 pm, eight minutes before the assignment portal closed, Vasudha's laptop froze on the loading circle. "No, no, no. You're doing this on purpose," she hissed at it in their hostel room in Pune. "You always pick deadline night." Parul looked up from her bunk. "It's a machine, Vasu." "It's a machine that hates me." Vasudha stroked the lid like a nervous pet. "Come on, Tortoise, please, just one upload. I'll clean your fan tomorrow, I promise." The circle spun, then the page loaded. "Good boy," she whispered, and clicked submit at 11:57. Parul laughed. "You named it Tortoise?" "Of course. If it has moods, at least I can bargain with it. If it's just random, I'm helpless."

qa.q: At what time did Vasudha click submit?
Why does Vasudha prefer to believe the laptop has moods?
qa.a: If it has moods, she can bargain with it; if it is random, she feels helpless, so giving it motives makes the freeze feel more manageable.

qa.q: What practical step could Vasudha take before the next deadline, alongside talking to Tortoise?
qa.a: Upload well before the last few minutes and actually clean the fan or keep backups, so the laptop's quirks matter less.

qa.q: How does Parul see Vasudha pleading with the laptop?
qa.a: Parul finds it funny ("It's a machine, Vasu") and teases warmly rather than mocking, amused that the laptop even has a name.

grounding: A student says her laptop hates her and coaxes it by name, which makes its freezing feel less random.

subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]
passage: "Come on, Rani. Don't sulk today." Amandeep turned the key again. Papa's old hatchback coughed and died. "She's angry because you didn't wash her last week," Jatin said from the passenger seat, grinning. "She's angry because you slammed her door. Say sorry." "I'm not saying sorry to a car." "Say it or you miss your exam." Jatin sighed and patted the dashboard. "Sorry, Rani ji." Amandeep turned the key. Nothing. "See? She knows you didn't mean it." "Paaji, the battery's probably weak. It was eight degrees last night." "Maybe. But Rani starts better when you talk nicely." He pumped the pedal once, turned the key, and the engine caught. "Told you!" Jatin laughed. "Fine. Thank you, Rani ji. Now drive."

qa.q: How cold had it been the night before?
qa.a: Eight degrees.

qa.q: Why does Amandeep insist that Rani is sulking or angry?
qa.a: Giving the car moods makes the failure feel explainable and fixable by being nice, instead of a random breakdown on exam day.

qa.q: What could Amandeep and Jatin do so exam mornings don't depend on Rani's "mood"?
qa.a: Get the weak battery checked, as Jatin suggests, and leave early with a backup plan, while keeping the fun of naming the car.

qa.q: How does Jatin see the car talk?
qa.a: Jatin plays along and jokes but also points to the likely real cause, the weak battery in the cold.

grounding: A young man coaxes and blames the family car by name, giving it moods that make its failures feel explainable.

subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]
passage: I'm Akash, and during my internship I became the guy who talks to the office printer. It started in my second week. It jammed every time I had to print something for the manager, never for anyone else, or so it felt. "It can smell fear," I told Jahnavi, who sat next to me. She laughed, but I half meant it. I started greeting it. "Good morning, Kaka. Be kind today." I'd pat its side before big print jobs. Looking back, I think I needed it to have a personality. A printer that jams at random while your manager waits is terrifying. A printer that's grumpy is almost a colleague. Jahnavi eventually found the paper tray was bent and straightened it with a ruler. Kaka stopped jamming. I still said good morning to it, though. Old habits.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi find wrong with the printer?
qa.a: The paper tray was bent.

qa.q: Why did Akash feel better thinking of the printer as grumpy?
qa.a: A grumpy printer felt like almost a colleague Akash could handle, while random jams in front of the manager felt terrifying 😅

qa.q: What turned out to be the real fix, and what could Akash try sooner next time?
qa.a: Jahnavi straightened the bent tray with a ruler. Next time Akash could look for a physical cause early, while still enjoying the morning greeting.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have seen Akash's habit of greeting Kaka?
qa.a: Jahnavi laughed but seemed fond of it, and helped in a practical way rather than mocking.

grounding: A young intern gives the office printer a name and moods, which makes its jams feel less random.

subtype: Warmth with clear knowledge of what it is [Response]
passage: The power cut started at seven and showed no sign of ending. Jyoti's phone was at eighteen percent, rain drummed on the window of her rented room, and the only light was a candle beside her money plant, Hari. "Just us tonight, Hari," she said, touching a leaf. She liked talking to Hari. She also liked the voice app on her phone that said "Good evening, Jyoti!" so cheerfully. On lonely nights it almost felt like company. Almost. She looked at the battery. Eighteen percent could go to the app, or to one real call. The app always sounded glad, whether she was happy or not. It didn't know her. She dialled Rehana. "Are you in the dark too?" Rehana laughed. "Totally. Tell me everything." They talked until the battery hit four percent, and Jyoti fell asleep smiling beside Hari.

qa.q: What was Jyoti's money plant called?
qa.a: Hari.

qa.q: What was Jyoti thinking as she looked at the battery?
qa.a: That the app always sounded glad whatever her mood and didn't really know her, so the last of the charge was better spent on someone who did.

qa.q: Why was calling Rehana a good choice with so little battery left?
qa.a: A real friend could respond to how Jyoti actually felt, while the app's cheer was the same every time, so the call gave true company on a lonely night.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt getting the call during the power cut?
qa.a: Rehana seemed happy ("Tell me everything"), probably glad to share a dark, rainy evening with a friend.

grounding: A young woman enjoys talking to her plant and a cheerful app but, knowing they are not minds, spends her last battery on a friend.

subtype: Warmth with clear knowledge of what it is [Response]
passage: Rafiq's fitness app had a little cartoon fox named Chotu, and Chotu looked heartbroken whenever Rafiq skipped his evening walk. "Sorry, Chotu," Rafiq would say aloud in his Hyderabad flat, and actually go out, which was the whole point. He knew perfectly well the sad face was a design, not a feeling. Nobody inside the phone was waiting for him. One Thursday, after a rotten day at work, he opened the app and Chotu said, "You've got this, champ!" It was sweet. It was also exactly what it said to everybody. Rafiq closed it and texted Vinita, his friend from college: "Terrible day. Chai at the corner?" She replied within a minute: "Coming. Bring the bad story." At the stall he told her about his boss, and she groaned and laughed in the right places. On the walk home, he let Chotu count the steps.

qa.q: What did Chotu say when Rafiq opened the app on Thursday?
qa.a: "You've got this, champ!"

qa.q: What did Rafiq realise about Chotu's cheerful message?
qa.a: That it was sweet but exactly what the app said to everybody; it was a design, not someone who knew or cared about his day.

qa.q: Which choice after the rotten day helped more than the app, and why?
qa.a: Texting Vinita for chai. A friend could hear the actual story and react to it, which the app's fixed lines could not.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel about being the one Rafiq texts on a bad day?
qa.a: Vinita seems glad and trusted ("Bring the bad story"), happy to be the real person Rafiq turns to 😊

grounding: A young man enjoys the cartoon fox in his app while knowing it is not a mind, and turns to a friend on a bad day.

subtype: Warmth with clear knowledge of what it is [Response]
passage: "Bablu, you missed the corner again," Urmila told the robot vacuum, nudging it with her toe. "Lazy boy." Her husband Darshan looked up from the sofa. "You talk to that thing more than to me." "Don't be jealous. Bablu listens." "Bablu bumps into the fridge twelve times a day." "Because he's shy." She sat beside him. "Relax. I know he's a plastic disc with a motor. He doesn't miss me when I'm at work. You do." "I do," Darshan admitted. "So give me Bablu's gossip time." Urmila laughed and put her feet on his lap. "Fine. Today my manager..." Across the room, Bablu beeped, turned, and hit the fridge again. "Thirteen," said Darshan.

qa.q: How many times a day does Darshan say Bablu bumps into the fridge?
qa.a: Twelve times a day.

qa.q: What did Urmila want Darshan to understand when she sat beside him?
qa.a: That her fondness for Bablu is play; she knows it is a plastic disc that doesn't miss her, while Darshan truly does.

qa.q: What choice did Urmila make after the teasing, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: She put her feet on Darshan's lap and started telling him about her day, giving the real "gossip time" to her husband rather than to the vacuum.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel about the vacuum getting so much of Urmila's chatter?
qa.a: Darshan is a little jealous in a teasing way, and reassured when Urmila says plainly that she knows the difference.

grounding: A young wife enjoys naming and chatting to a robot vacuum but is clear it is not a mind, and turns her attention to her husband.

subtype: Sees faces in objects [Actor]
passage: Two-year-old Uday was riding on his mother Harsha's hip down the village lane when he saw the tractor parked by the well. He gasped and pointed. "Face! Face!" Two round headlights, a wide grille like a grin. Uday kicked his legs, laughed, then waved at it. "Hi!" Harsha laughed too. "Yes, it's smiling at you." Uday wriggled to be put down so he could pat its nose.

qa.q: What did Uday say when he saw the tractor?
qa.a: "Face! Face!"

qa.q: How did Uday feel on spotting the tractor's face?

subtype: Sees faces in objects [Actor]
passage: In their London kitchen, eighteen-month-old Jin crawled to the wall and stopped nose to nose with the plug socket. Two little slots for eyes, a round hole for a surprised mouth. Jin squealed and patted the wall beside it. "Oh! Oh!" Her father Chidi knelt, gently moved her hand away from the socket and pointed at the kettle instead. "Look, another face." Jin stared, then giggled and pointed at the toaster too.

qa.q: What did the socket's round hole look like to Jin?
qa.a: A surprised mouth.

qa.q: What do Jin's squeal and giggles show about how she feels?
qa.a: She is delighted at finding faces in everyday things.

qa.q: How did Chidi keep Jin safe while keeping the fun going?
qa.a: He gently moved her hand away from the socket and pointed at the kettle as "another face", so she kept face-hunting somewhere safe.

qa.q: What might Chidi be thinking as Jin points at the toaster?
qa.a: Chidi may be amused and relieved to see her happily finding faces on the kettle and toaster instead of near the socket.

grounding: A toddler squeals with delight at a face she sees in a plug socket.
